docs.title: Developer API Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the Developer API portal.

These APIs provide a secure and scalable way to integrate with the platform, automate workflows, and exchange data between systems.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The APIs are designed to support:

  • Data import and export
  • Metadata management
  • Workflow automation
  • Integration with external systems

All APIs follow REST principles and use standard HTTP methods.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: APIs use Basic Authentication with an Access ID and Access Key.

docs.title: Steps to authenticate
docs.text:
1. Generate Access ID and Access Key from the application
  2. Encode credentials using Base64
  3. Include in request header

docs.title: Data Integration
docs.text:

  • Retrieve processed results

docs.title: Metadata Management
docs.text:
• Retrieve dimension details
  • Update hierarchies
  • Manage attributes

docs.title: Administration
docs.text:
• Retrieve system metadata
  • Monitor job status
  • Manage user access

docs.title: Data Load APIs
docs.text:
Used to import data into the platform.

API Description Load Data Upload data to staging Transfer Data Move data to destination Clear Data Remove staging data

docs.title: Data Retrieval APIs
docs.text:
Used to extract data for reporting and analysis.

API Description Get Data Retrieve transactional data Get Metadata Retrieve structure details Get Rules Retrieve configuration rules

Used for system-level operations.

API Description Login Authenticate user Get Session Retrieve session details Get Version Retrieve application version

docs.title: Documentation Strategy & Metrics
docs.text:
This page outlines my approach to building, scaling, and measuring enterprise SaaS documentation using a Docs-as-Code model.

The goal of documentation is not just completeness—but clarity, adoption, and measurable business impact.

docs.title: Documentation philosophy
docs.text: My documentation strategy is guided by four core principles.

docs.title: Docs are a product
docs.text: Documentation is treated as a first-class product with: - Clear ownership - Defined audiences - Roadmaps aligned to product releases - Quality and success metrics

docs.title: Audience-first information architecture
docs.text:
Content is intentionally layered to support different audiences:

  • Executives: What’s New, Release Highlights
  • End users: User Guides, How-To Guides
  • Support teams: FAQs, Troubleshooting
  • Product teams: Release Notes, UX Copy

Each layer answers a different question without duplicating content.

docs.title: Docs-as-Code for scale and quality
docs.text:
All documentation is managed using: - Git-based workflows - Markdown source files - Structured navigation - Version-controlled reviews

This approach enables faster updates, consistent formatting, peer reviews, and traceability across releases.

docs.title: Documentation supports adoption and deflection
docs.text: Documentation success is measured by how well it: - Enables users to complete tasks independently - Reduces support dependency - Improves feature adoption - Builds trust in the product

docs.title: Release-driven documentation
docs.text: Documentation planning is aligned with the product release cycle: - Release Notes and What’s New drafted in parallel with development - User Guides and How-To content updated for major workflows - UX copy reviewed before feature launch

docs.title: Ownership and quality standards
docs.text:
• Each product area has a designated documentation owner
  • Writers partner with Product, Engineering, UX, and Support
  • Standards ensure terminology consistency, task completeness, accessibility, and clear UX microcopy

docs.title: Content quality and efficiency
docs.text:
• Documentation throughput increase: ▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▱▱▱ 35%
  • Content quality score: ▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▱ 90%+
  • Support ticket deflection: ▰▰▰▰▰▰▱▱▱▱ 25%
  • Help engagement growth: ▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▱▱▱ 30% YoY

docs.title: Documentation lifecycle efficiency
docs.text:
Feature Design → UX Copy → Draft → Review → Publish → Measure → Improve

Documentation is created early, reviewed thoroughly, and continuously improved using real usage data.

How documentation flows through a release 1. Feature design: scope, users, and risks identified early 2. UX copy alignment: terminology finalized with design 3. Draft documentation: workflows documented in parallel 4. Review and validation: peer and SME feedback 5. Publish with release: docs ship with product 6. Measure and improve: analytics and support insights drive updates

docs.title: AI-assisted documentation modernization
docs.text: AI is used as a productivity accelerator, not a replacement for editorial judgment.

  • Terminology consistency across large doc sets

  • Human-in-the-loop governance for quality and accuracy

Documentation is continuously improved through analytics, support insights, audits, and post-release retrospectives.

A successful documentation strategy results in: - Faster user onboarding - Increased feature adoption - Reduced support load - Higher customer confidence - Strong Product–Enablement alignment

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: This section answers common questions related to forecasting, budgeting, and AI-assisted insights.

docs.title: Can I create multiple forecasts for the same period?
docs.text: Yes. You can create multiple forecast versions to model different scenarios and assumptions.

docs.title: Can forecasts be locked?
docs.text: Yes. Forecasts can be locked after submission to prevent further changes.

docs.title: Does AI change my data automatically?
docs.text: No. AI insights are advisory only. They highlight patterns and anomalies but do not modify values.

docs.title: How accurate are AI recommendations?
docs.text: AI insights are based on historical data patterns and should be reviewed alongside business context.

docs.title: Can multiple users work on the same forecast?
docs.text: Yes. Forecasting supports collaboration with role-based access and approval workflows.

docs.title: Is there an audit trail?
docs.text: Yes. All changes are tracked with user, timestamp, and value history.

docs.title: How does the platform handle large datasets?
docs.text: The platform is optimized for enterprise-scale data volumes and supports efficient recalculation and aggregation.

docs.title: How-To Guides
docs.text:
How-To Guides provide focused, task-based instructions for completing specific actions quickly and efficiently.

Each guide targets a single outcome.

docs.title: How to Create a Budget
docs.text: This guide walks you through creating a budget using forecast data and assumptions.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: Ensure that: - You have access to the planning workspace - Required dimensions (time, department, account) are available - A baseline forecast or actuals exist

docs.title: Step 1: Create a new budget version
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Planning > Budgets
  2. Select Create New Version
  3. Enter a name and description
  4. Choose the time period for the budget

docs.title: Step 2: Select a starting point
docs.text:
You can initialize a budget using: - Prior year actuals - Latest forecast version - A blank template

Select the option that best aligns with your planning approach.

docs.title: Step 3: Apply assumptions
docs.text:
Apply budget assumptions such as: - Percentage growth or reduction - Headcount changes - Seasonal adjustments

Assumptions can be applied globally or at a granular level.

docs.title: Step 4: Review AI insights (optional)
docs.text:
If enabled, AI insights may: - Flag values that deviate significantly from historical trends - Highlight areas requiring closer review

Use these insights to validate assumptions.

docs.title: Step 5: Submit for approval
docs.text: Once complete: 1. Review totals and summaries 2. Submit the budget for approval 3. Track approval status within the workflow

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: After approval, budgets can be: - Locked for reporting - Compared against actuals - Used as inputs for future forecasts

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: This section helps you resolve common issues related to forecasting and budgeting.

docs.title: Forecast values are not updating
docs.text:
Possible causes: - The forecast version is locked - Required drivers are missing - You do not have edit permissions

Resolution: - Verify version status - Check driver configuration - Confirm your access level

docs.title: AI insights are not visible
docs.text:
Possible causes: - AI features are disabled for your role - Insufficient historical data - Data refresh is incomplete

Resolution: - Contact an administrator - Ensure sufficient historical data exists - Retry after data refresh

docs.title: Approval workflow is blocked
docs.text:
Possible causes: - Pending approvals - Missing required reviewers

Resolution: - Review workflow status - Ensure all required approvers are assigned

docs.title: Performance issues when opening large forecasts
docs.text:
Possible causes: - Large dimensionality - Concurrent user activity

Resolution: - Filter data where possible - Work with administrators to optimize models

docs.title: Build a Forecast Scenario
docs.text:
This guide explains how to create forecast scenarios to evaluate different business outcomes under varying assumptions.

Forecast scenarios help teams model uncertainty and support data-driven decision-making.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a new forecast version
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Planning > Forecasts
  2. Select Create New Version
  3. Choose Scenario Forecast
  4. Enter a name and description

Use clear naming to distinguish scenarios (for example, Best Case or Conservative).

docs.title: Step 2: Select a baseline
docs.text:
Choose a starting point: - Latest approved forecast - Approved budget - Actuals-to-date

Baselines ensure consistency across scenarios.

docs.title: Step 3: Apply scenario-specific assumptions
docs.text:
Adjust assumptions such as: - Revenue growth rates - Headcount changes - Cost increase or reduction

Assumptions can be applied globally or at a granular level.

docs.title: Step 4: Review AI-assisted insights
docs.text:
AI insights may: - Highlight unusual variances - Surface potential forecast risks - Identify areas that require closer review

Insights are advisory and should be reviewed alongside business context.

docs.title: Step 5: Save and validate
docs.text: Save the scenario and review validation messages. Resolve any issues before proceeding.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
After creating scenarios, review results and submit the selected forecast for approval.

docs.title: Forecasting Overview
docs.text:
This guide provides an overview of the forecasting capabilities available in the platform and explains how finance teams can create, manage, and refine forecasts at scale.

Forecasting is designed for enterprise planning scenarios where accuracy, auditability, and collaboration are critical.

docs.title: What you can do with Forecasting
docs.text:
Using Forecasting, you can:

  • Create rolling and static forecasts across time horizons
  • Model multiple forecast scenarios for comparison
  • Incorporate historical actuals and assumptions
  • Collaborate across finance and business teams
  • Leverage AI-assisted insights to identify trends and anomalies

docs.title: Forecast versions
docs.text: Forecasts are created as versions, allowing you to: - Maintain a baseline forecast - Create alternative scenarios (Best Case, Worst Case) - Lock versions for audit and reporting purposes

docs.title: Driver-based forecasting
docs.text:
Driver-based models allow forecast values to be calculated using: - Growth rates - Headcount drivers - Volume-based assumptions

This approach improves consistency and reduces manual effort.

docs.title: AI-assisted forecasting insights
docs.text:
AI-assisted forecasting analyzes historical data and forecast inputs to: - Highlight unusual variances - Surface potential risks early - Suggest adjustment areas based on past patterns

These insights are advisory and do not modify forecast values automatically.

docs.title: Governance and controls

Use summary views to identify areas requiring attention.

Address these items before submission.

docs.text: The Create Forecast Scenario Variants feature allows users to generate multiple versions of a base forecast scenario. This helps analyze different assumptions, compare outcomes, and support decision-making through structured scenario planning.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the Forecasting module.
  2. Select an existing forecast scenario to use as the base.
  3. Click Create Variant.
  4. Enter a name and description for the variant.
  5. Modify key inputs such as assumptions, drivers, or time periods.
  6. Save the variant.
  7. Repeat the process to create additional variants as needed.
  8. Use the Version Comparison feature to review differences across variants.
  9. Submit the preferred variant for approval.

docs.title: Tips and best practices
docs.text:
• Use a consistent naming convention to identify variants easily.
  • Clearly document the assumptions for each variant.
  • Limit the number of changes per variant for clearer analysis.
  • Regularly compare variants to track impact of changes.
  • Validate data before submitting for approval.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:

  • Comparison issues: Confirm that variants are aligned in structure and time period.
  • Approval not progressing: Check if the correct approver is assigned.
  • Unexpected results: Review modified assumptions and input data.END

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Forecast Scenario Sensitivity Analysis helps you quantify how changes in key drivers (price, volume, costs, FX, interest rates, churn, etc.) affect outcomes such as revenue, EBITDA, cash flow, and valuation. Use it to test scenarios, identify value drivers, and prioritize actions under uncertainty.

docs.title: Who should use this
docs.text:
• Financial analysts and FP&A teams building and stress-testing forecasts
  • Corporate development and treasury evaluating valuation and liquidity risk
  • Business partners comparing plans, risks, and upside cases

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Access to the forecasting model with edit rights
  • A validated baseline forecast (assumptions, time horizon, currency)
  • Defined target metrics (e.g., Revenue, EBITDA, FCF, NPV)
  • Mapped drivers to model logic (no broken links or circular references)
  • Historical data and driver ranges or distributions
  • Version control or a workspace for scenario copies

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Clarify the objective
  2. Define the question (e.g., “What drives variance in FY revenue?”).

  3. Select output metrics (KPIs) and time buckets (monthly/quarterly/annual).

  4. Set the baseline

  5. Load the latest approved forecast.

  6. Lock the version and note key baseline values for chosen KPIs.

  7. Select drivers and ranges

  8. Choose 3–10 drivers with clear causal links to outputs.

  9. For each driver, set:

    • Type: deterministic (single value/range) or stochastic (distribution).
    • Range: min/base/max or confidence interval.
    • Constraints: floors/ceilings, integer-only, sign limits.

  10. Create scenarios

  11. Base Case: unchanged baseline.
  12. Upside/Downside: apply coherent, business-justified changes across drivers.

  13. Edge/Stress: apply extreme but plausible shocks to test resilience.

  14. Run one-way sensitivity

  15. Vary one driver across its range; hold others constant.

  16. Capture output changes; produce a sensitivity curve for each KPI.

  17. Run two-way sensitivity (optional)

  18. Select two interacting drivers (e.g., price and volume).

  19. Create a grid of combinations; visualize impact heatmap on KPIs.

  20. Generate a tornado chart

  21. Rank drivers by their marginal impact on a target KPI over the set range.

  22. Identify top value/risk contributors.

  23. Run Monte Carlo (if available)

  24. Assign distributions (e.g., normal for demand error, triangular for cost).
  25. Set trials (e.g., 5,000–20,000) and random seed for reproducibility.

  26. Review percentile bands (P10/P50/P90), probability of loss/covenant breach.

  27. Compare scenarios

  28. Use side-by-side KPI tables and variance waterfalls vs. baseline.

  29. Attribute variance by driver and by time period.

  30. Validate and document

    • Sanity-check outputs (signs, magnitudes, timing).
    • Record assumptions, ranges, and rationale in scenario notes.

  31. Export and share

    • Save scenario versions with clear names and dates.
    • Export charts/tables to your reporting pack.
    • Share links or schedule refreshes if supported.

  32. Iterate

    • Refine ranges based on insights.
    • Narrow to the few drivers that explain most variance.
    • Align recommendations with risk appetite and target outcomes.

docs.title: Tips and best practices
docs.text:
• Start simple: test a small set of high-impact drivers before expanding.
  • Use realistic ranges anchored in history, contracts, or market data.
  • Separate correlation from causation; avoid double-counting related drivers.
  • Keep time granularity consistent across inputs and outputs.
  • Document every assumption; use versioned scenario names (e.g., FY27_Upside_v3).
  • Stress liquidity first: include working capital, capex timing, and covenants.
  • Standardize charts: tornado for drivers, fan charts for distributions, waterfalls for variance explanation.
  • Calibrate distributions from forecasting errors or external benchmarks.
  • Lock formulas and map drivers to single sources of truth to prevent drift.
  • Backtest: run the method on prior periods to check realism.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Outputs do not change when drivers move
  • Cause: Driver not linked to model or overwritten by hardcode.

  • Fix: Trace dependencies; replace hardcodes with formulas; refresh links.

  • Implausible or negative results

  • Cause: Missing floors/ceilings or unit mismatches.

  • Fix: Add constraints; align units (%, bps, currency); validate signs.

  • Circular reference or calculation errors

  • Cause: Feedback loops (e.g., interest depends on cash, which depends on interest).

  • Fix: Use iterative calc with limits, or restructure to break loops.

  • Monte Carlo runs are slow or unstable

  • Cause: Too many trials or volatile distributions.

  • Fix: Reduce trials, simplify model, set random seed, cap tails.

  • Heatmaps/tornado charts look inconsistent

  • Cause: Mixed time horizons or different KPI definitions.

  • Fix: Standardize periods and KPI formulas across scenarios.

  • Scenario names overwrite prior work

  • Cause: Duplicate naming.

  • Fix: Enforce naming convention with timestamps and owner tags.

  • Exported results don’t match dashboard

  • Cause: Unsaved scenario or stale cache.

  • Fix: Save and recalc before export; clear cache; confirm filter context.

  • Ranges exceed business constraints

  • Cause: Unbounded inputs.

  • Fix: Add business rules (e.g., churn ≤ 100%, price ≥ floor).

  • Long run times after adding drivers

  • Cause: Over-parameterization.

  • Fix: Prioritize top drivers; aggregate less material lines; precompute lookups.

  • Permission or access error

  • Cause: Insufficient rights to scenarios or drivers.
  • Fix: Request edit access; check workspace and role settings.

docs.title: Forecasting Overview
docs.text:
This guide provides an overview of the forecasting capabilities available in the platform and explains how finance teams can create, manage, and refine forecasts at scale.

Forecasting is designed for enterprise planning scenarios where accuracy, auditability, and collaboration are critical.

docs.title: What you can do with Forecasting
docs.text:
Using Forecasting, you can:

  • Create rolling and static forecasts across time horizons
  • Model multiple forecast scenarios for comparison
  • Incorporate historical actuals and assumptions
  • Collaborate across finance and business teams
  • Leverage AI-assisted insights to identify trends and anomalies

docs.title: Forecast versions
docs.text: Forecasts are created as versions, allowing you to: - Maintain a baseline forecast - Create alternative scenarios (Best Case, Worst Case) - Lock versions for audit and reporting purposes

docs.title: Driver-based forecasting
docs.text:
Driver-based models allow forecast values to be calculated using: - Growth rates - Headcount drivers - Volume-based assumptions

This approach improves consistency and reduces manual effort.

docs.title: AI-assisted forecasting insights
docs.text:
AI-assisted forecasting analyzes historical data and forecast inputs to: - Highlight unusual variances - Surface potential risks early - Suggest adjustment areas based on past patterns

These insights are advisory and do not modify forecast values automatically.

docs.title: Governance and controls

docs.title: When to use Forecasting

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Review Scenario Analysis is the process of evaluating and validating different forecast scenarios to understand their impact on financial outcomes. It involves comparing multiple scenarios, analyzing key variances, and assessing underlying assumptions to ensure accuracy and reliability. This step helps stakeholders identify risks, make informed decisions, and select the most appropriate forecast before final approval.

docs.title: Who should use this
docs.text:
• FP&A analysts and finance managers
  • Business unit leaders and product owners
  • Strategy and corporate development teams
  • Risk management and treasury
  • Executive reviewers and approvers

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Clearly defined scenarios (e.g., Base, Upside, Downside) with unique names or IDs
  • A baseline or prior-approved forecast to compare against
  • Access to the financial model or planning tool and required data sources
  • Defined key performance indicators (KPIs) and reporting currency (e.g., revenue, gross margin, EBITDA, cash flow, headcount, CapEx)
  • An assumptions register covering key drivers (pricing, volume, churn, FX, inflation, hiring, seasonality)
  • Agreed fiscal calendar and time horizon (e.g., monthly/quarterly for 12–24 months)
  • Variance thresholds and acceptance criteria (e.g., investigate any >5% or >$X variance)
  • Version control plan and collaboration channels for stakeholder review

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Define scope and objectives
  2. Clarify the decision to be supported (e.g., budget approval, investment, hiring plan).

  3. Confirm the period, granularity, and KPIs to evaluate.

  4. Assemble scenarios

  5. Collect scenario files or versions from the planning tool.

  6. Verify each scenario includes consistent timeframes and complete data for all KPIs.

  7. Validate data integrity

  8. Check for missing periods, duplicates, or broken links.
  9. Reconcile totals to source systems where applicable.

  10. Ensure currency, units, and calendars are consistent.

  11. Set evaluation criteria and thresholds

  12. Document quantitative thresholds for investigation (absolute and percentage).

  13. Define qualitative criteria (e.g., plausibility of assumptions, alignment with strategy).

  14. Normalize and run scenarios

  15. Ensure common modeling settings (e.g., FX rates, calendar, accounting rules).

  16. Recalculate or refresh all scenarios to eliminate stale outputs.

  17. Compare scenarios using variance analysis

  18. Calculate period-by-period and year-to-date variances vs. baseline and vs. each other.
  19. Use absolute and percentage variances, plus contribution analysis by driver, product, or region.

  20. Create bridges (waterfalls) to show sources of change between scenarios.

  21. Examine key drivers and assumptions

  22. Review the assumptions register for each scenario.
  23. Test plausibility: source, date, owner, method, and historical back-testing.

  24. Check dependencies (e.g., price-volume, headcount-productivity) for logical consistency.

  25. Perform sensitivity and stress testing

  26. Vary critical drivers within reasonable ranges to test robustness.
  27. Run stress cases for tail risks (e.g., demand shock, supply constraint, FX swing).

  28. Note breakpoints where results change materially.

  29. Assess risks, mitigations, and contingencies

  30. Identify top risks per scenario and quantify potential impact.

  31. Document mitigations, trigger points, and contingency actions.

  32. Document findings

  33. Summarize key variances, drivers, and rationale for differences.
  34. Highlight assumptions that most influence outcomes.

  35. Provide a clear narrative and executive summary.

  36. Review with stakeholders

  37. Share results, methods, and assumptions for feedback.

  38. Capture and resolve challenges, questions, and requested reruns.

  39. Recommend and select a scenario

  40. Evaluate scenarios against criteria and risk tolerance.
  41. Provide a reasoned recommendation with sensitivities and caveats.

  42. Obtain sign-off from approvers.

  43. Finalize and archive

  44. Lock the approved scenario in the planning tool with version tags.
  45. Archive inputs, calculations, and documentation for auditability.
  46. Record lessons learned for future cycles.

docs.title: Tips and best practices
docs.text:
• Establish a standard scenario taxonomy (e.g., Base, Conservative, Aggressive) and naming convention.
  • Use a consistent KPI set and time buckets to ensure like-for-like comparisons.
  • Apply materiality thresholds to focus analysis on impactful variances.
  • Visualize results with bridges and trend charts to clarify drivers.
  • Keep an up-to-date assumptions register with owners, sources, and timestamps.
  • Perform quick sanity checks (unit economics, seasonality, cohort metrics) before deep dives.
  • Involve cross-functional SMEs early (sales, ops, HR, supply chain) to validate realism.
  • Differentiate structural vs. timing variances; flag one-offs and non-recurring items.
  • Document unresolved uncertainties and define decision trigger points.
  • Maintain version control; change-log any model or assumption updates.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Variances appear unrealistic or volatile
  • Check for inconsistent time granularity, calendar mismatches, or FX settings.

  • Recalculate scenarios and clear cached results.

  • Scenarios use different assumptions unknowingly

  • Compare assumptions registers side-by-side.

  • Standardize global settings (inflation, FX, accounting rules) and rerun.

  • Data gaps or broken links

  • Identify missing periods or entities; repair source connections.

  • Backfill with the latest actuals or approved proxies and document.

  • Conflicting KPI movements (e.g., revenue up, margin unexpectedly down)

  • Decompose drivers (price, mix, discounting, COGS inflation).

  • Review dependencies and constraints in the model.

  • Sensitivity tests produce unstable outputs

  • Reduce step sizes and test one driver at a time.

  • Inspect formulas for circular references or hardcoded overrides.

  • Stakeholders challenge credibility

  • Provide traceability: sources, methods, and historical back-tests.

  • Share scenario bridges and sensitivity results; note limitations transparently.

  • Approval delays due to unresolved questions

  • Log open issues with owners and due dates.
  • Propose interim decision criteria and escalation paths.

docs.title: What’s New
docs.text:
This section provides a high-level summary of key product updates introduced in each release.

What’s New is designed for: - Executives and business leaders - Product and enablement teams - Customers who want a quick overview of value

Each update focuses on outcomes and impact, not implementation detail.

For full technical information, refer to the Release Notes.

docs.title: What’s New in 2025.10
docs.text: The 2025.10 release delivers foundational improvements across forecasting and budgeting workflows.

docs.title: Improved budget initialization options
docs.text:
Budgets can now be created using multiple starting points, including actuals and forecasts.

Why it matters: Greater flexibility in how teams start planning.

docs.title: Clearer submission status indicators
docs.text:
Users can easily see whether budgets and forecasts are draft, submitted, or approved.

Why it matters: Reduces confusion and improves accountability.

docs.title: What’s New in 2025.11
docs.text: The 2025.11 release focuses on usability and planning efficiency.

docs.title: Simplified forecast setup
docs.text:
Creating new forecasts is now faster, with clearer setup steps and defaults.

Why it matters: Teams spend less time configuring and more time planning.

docs.title: Better validation and error feedback

Improved validation messages guide users when inputs are missing or invalid.

Why it matters: Reduces rework and improves data quality.

docs.title: More responsive user experience

docs.text:

Why it matters: Stronger auditability supports compliance and trust in the numbers.

docs.title: Improved collaboration through comments

Why it matters: Fewer side conversations and clearer decision context.

docs.title: Initial AI-assisted insights

AI-assisted insights provide early visibility into forecast trends and outliers.

Why it matters: Teams gain an additional layer of analysis without extra effort.

docs.title: Governance enhancements

docs.title: What’s New in 2026.1
docs.text: The 2026.1 release focuses on improving forecast confidence, decision-making speed, and governance across planning cycles.

docs.title: Smarter forecasting with AI-assisted insights
docs.text:

Why it matters: Teams spend less time tracking approvals and more time analyzing results.
